R3-01.why: Four mechanically distinct phases, each close to a small game of its own. There are two physics-comedy sandboxes (client debris plus a server evidence state machine over about 25 objects), a separate arcade lane-dodge driving game, a tap-to-hide system over 60 spots with random subsets and decoys, and a hunt with 3 gadgets (scent trails, residue, FREEZE). On top of that come a naughty-step mini-loop, Report Card posing, an AI Parent with pathfinding and search logic for the practice house, a Bedroom housing and furniture system with gifting, mastery tracks, a Feats log and a ranked ladder. The hardest problem is FREEZE: it judges movement inside the Parent's view on client-owned characters under varying ping. Too lenient and it feels broken; too strict and kids get caught unfairly. Snitch and re-hide also need careful server state. Content is heavy: a densely dressed interactive house with 25 breakable evidence props, 60 hide spots and a second practice house. It needs 5–7 players a server with asymmetric roles, which makes low-CCU matchmaking and role-queue fairness harder than in the co-op concepts. 3–4 months is not realistic with this scope.
R3-01.fix: Cut the driving mini-game: show the Parent a 20 s arrival map or gossip-pick screen instead. Cut Bedroom housing (use a static trophy shelf), the AI Parent (use a scripted tutorial), Snitch and Decoy. Ship only the Sniff and FREEZE gadgets. At launch, aim for 1 house, 15 evidence objects and 30 hide spots.

R3-02.why: A single static tower arena with no locomotion and no camera control removes most character networking and anti-exploit work. Enemies are server lane data rendered on clients, which is cheap and authoritative. It is solo-playable at 1–4 players, so it has no matchmaking dependency. Gesture recognition is a known, small algorithm ($1/$P recognizer, about 200 lines of Luau). Stroke points are resampled and validated on the server. The 1 s fusion window is decided by server receive time, which tolerates normal ping. The hardest problem is classifier feel across devices: finger vs mouse, small phones and frame-rate-dependent sampling all affect it, and a generous 'partial power' band hides misclassification. The console radial is a second input path to build and test. The real cost is VFX and balance volume: 6 runes, 6 misfire gags, 12 bespoke fusions, a boss and relics that each change fusion behaviour (a combinatorial test matrix). Ink-colour mixing inside fusions adds shader and particle work. All of this is achievable.
R3-02.fix: At launch, cap fusions at 8 and use relics that adjust numeric parameters (size, duration, chain count) rather than adding new behaviour. Drop the console radial until after launch. Use one shared misfire gag pool instead of a gag per rune.

R3-03.why: It is built on standard Roblox character movement and well-trodden hide-and-seek and asymmetric patterns. The beam cone test is a cheap server-side check, freeze poses are static animations, the NPC statues are simple timed pose swaps, and pranks are a handful of tagged objects with discrete states. The launch scope (1 museum, 3 wings, R15 statues, 8 pranks, still snapshots) is concrete and sized sensibly. The hardest problem is fair tagging: deciding 'moved while lit' on client-owned characters. That needs server position history, ping-scaled grace, speed and teleport sanity checks, and must work alongside the 'snap to nearest plinth' teleport. The disguise system also takes care: it must override player avatars to uniform statue appearance (HumanoidDescription and material stripping, hiding accessories) and spawn matching NPC skins. Without it the hide-in-plain-sight premise leaks. Asymmetric 1v4–7 balance tuning (battery, wing locks, mischief rate), revive and cracked-statue loops, abilities and the Unmasking reel add moderate breadth. 1vN servers of 5–8 also raise the matchmaking fill burden at low CCU.
R3-03.fix: At launch, drop statue abilities and hidden pranks. Make wing locks scripted on a timer rather than tied to battery. Run 4–6-player servers with bot-filled NPC statues and a bot Guard fallback only for the tutorial.

R3-04.why: The cleanest technical stance in the set. The raft is a server-side kinematic controller on a spline at 20–30 Hz with client interpolation: no physics ownership and nothing to exploit beyond rate-limited button inputs. Blame-card input timelines, friend ghost rafts (recorded spline parameter, offset and heading) and daily-seed leaderboards (OrderedDataStore) fall out of the server's input log almost for free. Animation is minimal: paddle and bail loops plus emotes. It is playable at 2 players, which makes low-CCU matchmaking easier. The hardest problem is how the core control feels under latency. Every seat's input reaches the server with a different ping, so the combined heading lags 100–250 ms. That needs local predicted feedback for your own paddle and generous hazard tolerances, or it feels mushy. Versus adds custom raft-vs-raft collision and bump resolution inside the kinematic model, plus water-balloon and bail-into-rival interactions. Content is moderate: 12 river segments with branches, ramps and hazards need a modular river and spline toolkit and level-design iteration. Each new vehicle (sky balloon = altitude axis) is a new controller variant, so update cost per vehicle is non-trivial.
R3-04.fix: At launch, ship 8 segments built from a modular piece kit. Make versus 2 rafts only, with simple circle-push bumps. Postpone non-yaw vehicles such as the balloon until the controller is stable.

R3-05.why: Many interacting simulation systems. It needs a procedural house from modular rooms with a navmesh that stays valid, a server fire-spread grid that has to replicate (delta-encoded) and interact with fire types (grease/foam, electrical/breaker), and a hose sweep with magnetism that must be checked on the server. Add a water tank and hydrants, timed floor collapse that changes geometry and pathing, downed-teammate drag, and a carry system (welded critters, wriggle-free, two-player carry). The hardest problem is critter AI in a dynamic environment: hide, flee from fire, panic and escape-mayhem behaviours with pathfinding through a procedurally built, burning, collapsing house, all running on the server for 1–4 players while staying cheap on low-end mobile (smoke and particle budget). Assets and animation are the second big cost: 20–40 critters on 2 shared rigs still means 40 skinned meshes plus rig animation sets, accessory fitting across body shapes, and companion follow and ride-on-truck logic. The launch scope is honestly trimmed (one building, no sanctuary), but the core run alone is a mid-to-large production for 3–4 months.
R3-05.fix: Hand-author 3 house layouts instead of generating them. Use a simple state-machine critter AI (hide spot → flee-to-exit) with no free pathing during collapse. Ship 15 critters on 2 rigs, and drop two-player carry and the escaped-critter mayhem until after launch.

overall_notes: Ranking by simplicity: R3-02 ≈ R3-04 (7) > R3-03 (6) > R3-05 (4) > R3-01 (3). The two highest-scoring concepts avoid client-owned character judgement: R3-02 has a static arena with server lane enemies, and R3-04 has a server kinematic raft. Both are also playable at 1–2 players, which removes most low-CCU matchmaking risk. Their remaining risks are feel tuning (gesture classifier; input-latency mush) and content and VFX volume, not architecture. R3-03 is standard tech, but its fairness depends on lag-compensated judgement of client-owned characters, and it needs 1vN fill. R3-05 and R3-01 stack too many bespoke systems. R3-05 needs procedural building, a fire grid, critter AI and 40 rigged creatures. R3-01 is effectively 4 mini-games plus housing plus an AI Parent. Neither ships a compelling first version in 3–4 months without the cuts listed.
